title: Migrants: Building a Country and Dying in It
author: Diego Torres
content:
_This article by Diego Torres appears in the November 2026 issue of_ Let's
Talk About Migration _(_ Hablemos de Migración _), a magazine on migration
issues published by the Frente Amplio de Mexicanos y Migrantes.[Read and
download the full November
issue](https://diegotorres72.com/internacional/boletin-hablemos-de-
migracion-2/)._

![Let's Talk About Migration](https://mexicosolidarity.com/wp-
content/uploads/2025/06/image-1.png)

The deaths of migrants during Donald Trump's second term have been a prominent
topic in both the media and diplomatic exchanges between the migrants'
countries of origin and the U.S. government. However, the fact that they are
currently making headlines does not mean this is a new phenomenon. All empires
are built upon the backs of millions who have lost their lives in their
construction; in ancient times they were slaves, today they are migrants.

History doesn't repeat itself because it's inevitable or because people are
ignorant of it; it repeats itself because the powerful repeats it. The idea of
democracy is sold, but the conditions don't exist for the population to truly
decide. The powerful pull the strings of who gets into government positions.
And to keep people passive, they use fear as one of their main tools.

On the one hand, sectors of the middle class are being frightened by the claim
that migrants will take their jobs, even though the reality of the labor
market shows a considerable dependence on migrant labor in certain sectors. In
2025, the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics recorded a proportionally larger
presence of foreign-born workers in services, construction, maintenance,
manufacturing, and transportation. Among undocumented migrants, this presence
is even more visible: the Pew Research Center estimated that in 2023 they
represented 24% of agricultural workers and 19% of those working in
construction occupations.

Migrants, both documented and undocumented, are also kept immobilized by the
fear of detention and deportation. All of this occurs while a few individuals
manage to amass unimaginable fortunes. Elon Musk, for example, recently
unveiled a new Tesla Roadster as a flying car amidst the news of becoming the
world's first trillionaire. As a satirical irony, we might ask what good a
flying car is in the face of the poverty that persists on the streets of the
United States.

The Trump administration, with its constant pursuit of publicity, helps us see
a problem that has been intertwined with American history: the deaths of
migrants. Throughout U.S. history, the deaths of migrants in the construction
and expansion of the country have rarely been a central focus of public
discourse.

When the transcontinental railroad was built, it was Chinese migrants who
performed the most dangerous labor. Information from the U.S. National Park
Service shows an estimate that more than a thousand Chinese workers died. And
as if that weren't enough, after construction was completed, as a token of
gratitude, the U.S. government passed the Chinese Exclusion Act in 1882, the
first major federal law to restrict immigration from a specific national group
and prohibit the entry of Chinese workers for years.

During the Bracero Program, deaths of Mexican workers were also documented.
One of the most serious cases occurred on September 17, 1963, in Chualar,
California, when a vehicle transporting farm workers collided with a freight
train. Thirty-two Mexican braceros died. The accident was even addressed that
same year in the U.S. Congress.

![Migrants: Building a Country and Dying in
It](https://mexicosolidarity.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/ltam-
nov26-03-body-p13.jpg)Illustration: _Let 's Talk About Migration_, November
2026

It is clear that we are currently discussing a different context: deaths
occurring while in the custody of a government agency or during immigration
operations. But looking back allows us to understand the importance of
migrants in the construction, history, and life of the United States.

The current death toll during Trump's second term also reveals something else.
In the early years of U.S. immigration history, Chinese workers were victims
of intense xenophobia that even became federal legislation. Today, Mexicans,
due to the size and long-standing presence of their community in the United
States, face considerable exposure to current detention and deportation
policies.

Since Trump's return to the White House, a large portion of deportations
initially focused on people apprehended after crossing the border. An analysis
published in October 2026 by the Associated Press indicates that 69% of
deportations carried out between January 2025 and July 2026 involved people
initially intercepted at the southern border.

Within these policies, Venezuelans, Haitians and Cubans, among many other
nationalities, have also been affected. But as operations move deeper into
communities, people who have been living in the United States for many years
are exposed, some with families, jobs and a life built over decades.

And it is here that the Mexican migrant community faces grave danger. Although
the Mexican government has sent diplomatic notes regarding the violence and
the deaths of 17 Mexicans linked to the immigration detention system, on
October 18, 2026, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs confirmed the death of yet
another Mexican national—this time at the Rio Grande Processing Center in
Laredo, Texas. This incident brings the total number of Mexicans who have died
while in custody or during immigration operations since January 20, 2025, to
18.

Those in power will continue to intimidate the population—a tactic that has
served them well for many years. Yet, in the current climate—where migrants
are criminalized, persecuted, detained, and deported, and where some have even
lost their lives while in custody or during immigration enforcement
operations—only one path remains for migrants: organization and protest.

The significance of migrants is profound. This is evidenced by the history of
the railroads, the development of our cities, the realities of the American
agricultural sector, and the structure of today’s economy. It is therefore
essential that migrants themselves recognize their own worth and, at last,
make their voices heard.
